summary: Describes version 1.1 of Ipsilon's General Switch Management Protocol, a general-purpose protocol that lets a controller set up and release connections on an ATM switch and read its status. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: GSMP lets a controller tell an ATM switch how to connect virtual channels and manage ports. The switch can reply to requests and report events such as a port changing state.

subtitle: A master-slave protocol for a controller to manage connections and ports on an ATM switch.

tldr.problem: A controller needs a way to create and remove ATM switch connections, manage ports, and request switch information.
tldr.mechanism: GSMP sends controller requests to a switch over an ATM control connection. The peers first synchronize with an adjacency protocol, then exchange requests, responses, and switch event messages.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1987 describes GSMP version 1.1 as an Informational document. It has been updated by RFC 2297.

today: RFC 1987 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 2297.

sections.title: The Controller and the Switch
sections.content:
The General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP) controls an ATM switch. A controller can establish or release connections, manage ports, and request configuration or statistics. The switch can also report asynchronous events such as a link going down.

The protocol is asymmetric: the controller is the master and the switch is the slave. GSMP runs across an ATM link on a control virtual channel established during initialization. A controller can manage multiple switches using separate protocol instances.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller gives instructions to a switch, and the switch reports whether each request worked. The switch can also send a notice when something changes without being asked.

sections.title: Messages and Request Tracking
sections.content:
GSMP messages are carried in AAL-5 CPCS-PDUs with an LLC/SNAP header. The RFC sets the GSMP message MTU to 1500 octets and gives a default control virtual channel of VPI 0 and VCI 15.

Most messages share a header with a version, message type, result, code, and transaction identifier. The transaction identifier lets the controller match a response to its request. A request can ask for a success response or only receive a response if it fails; event messages from the switch are not acknowledged.

Except for adjacency messages, GSMP messages must not be sent until the adjacency protocol has synchronized the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ordinary GSMP message has a label that tells what it is and a transaction number that connects a reply to its request. Before using these messages, the controller and switch must synchronize.

sections.title: Creating and Removing Connections
sections.content:
Connection-management messages let the controller add or delete a branch, remove a whole connection, verify a connection, delete all connections on an input port, or move a branch. A connection maps an incoming ATM virtual channel to one or more outgoing virtual channels.

GSMP treats a connection with one output branch as unicast and one with multiple output branches as multicast. Adding a second branch for the same input extends the connection; deleting its last branch removes it. Requests include a port session number so a switch can reject a request referring to an outdated port state.
sections.plainLanguage: A request names an incoming virtual channel and the outgoing channel or channels it should reach. Adding more outgoing branches makes the switch copy traffic to more destinations.

sections.title: Port Management, Statistics, and Events
sections.content:
Port-management messages can bring a port up or down, set loopback behavior, reset an input port, or clear event flags. Statistics messages report virtual-channel activity, port statistics, or virtual-channel statistics. Configuration messages let the controller learn switch and port capabilities.

The switch can send event messages such as Port Up, Port Down, Invalid VPI/VCI, New Port, or Dead Port. It sends these without waiting for an acknowledgment. The RFC also defines failure responses that return the request with a code explaining why it failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller can ask for port settings and traffic counts, and the switch can send notices about changes. A failure reply includes a code that gives more detail about the problem.

sections.title: Synchronizing the Adjacency
sections.content:
The adjacency protocol synchronizes state across the control link, identifies the entity at the other end, and detects when it changes. Its messages use codes such as SYN, SYNACK, ACK, and RSTACK.

Each end tracks adjacency state and exchanges periodic messages. When the peer's identity or instance information does not match, the protocol can reset synchronization. Only after the link is synchronized can the peers exchange other GSMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller and switch first exchange messages to confirm who is on the other end and that both sides are ready. Regular GSMP instructions wait until this check is complete.
